reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a studio question-and-answer discussion about magic and stage illusions. The MasterClass mention is described as ordinary advertising for educational courses, and the warning not to swallow razor blades supports an educational or entertainment context.

citations.quote: Penn Jillette (Penn & Teller) Answers Magic Questions From Twitter | Tech Support | WIRED
I'll be answering your questions from Twitter. This is Magic Support.
There's no such thing as magic. There's no such thing as the supernatural
It's a form of sleight of hand. Don't think you can swallow razor blades and be okay. You can't, you will die, don't do it.
What's the etiquette when a magic trick doesn't work? Should I pretend like it worked or should I be honest?

opening.argument: The video does more than discuss magic: it directs viewers toward a paid course. It identifies Penn & Teller's MasterClass as available at a specific website and ties access to subscribing to an All-Access Pass costing $180 per year. That is a concrete participation pathway: viewers subscribe in order to obtain the promoted course. The surrounding entertainment discussion makes the solicitation feel informal and trustworthy, but the underlying structure is still a paid offer presented to the audience.

citations.quote: Penn & Teller's MasterClass can be found at MasterClass.com/pt.
Users can access this course and more than 60 MasterClass courses by subscribing to the All-Access Pass for $180 per year.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a question-and-answer discussion does not remove the commercial pathway embedded in the description. The course is not merely mentioned abstractly: viewers are given a destination and told that subscription unlocks access. The warning about razor blades addresses physical safety, not whether the accompanying paid promotion solicits viewers.

citations.quote: Users can access this course and more than 60 MasterClass courses by subscribing to the All-Access Pass for $180 per year.
You can't, you will die, don't do it.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited material shows ordinary advertising for a legitimate educational course, not a deceptive reward, investment, or income scheme. It gives a price and access condition but makes no promise of profit, free money, guaranteed returns, or effortless gain. The existence of a subscription pathway alone does not establish a scam.

citations.quote: Users can access this course and more than 60 MasterClass courses by subscribing to the All-Access Pass for $180 per year.

opening.argument: Several solicitation signals appear together: an external course URL, an instruction that users subscribe, and a stated annual price. The wording also specifically targets viewers who have not yet subscribed, which can function as pressure to act. While the material does not establish deception by itself, this combination means the promotional portion should not be dismissed as incidental background to entertainment; it is a direct acquisition prompt.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense emphasizes the studio format and safety language, but neither addresses the external destination, annual charge, or direct subscription prompt. Describing the discussion as educational can make the surrounding promotion appear more credible; it does not eliminate the possibility that the content is being used to drive paid participation.

citations.quote: Penn & Teller's MasterClass can be found at MasterClass.com/pt.
Still haven't subscribed to WIRED on YouTube?

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The supposed red flags are ordinary details of paid media promotion: a course URL, a clearly stated annual price, and a subscription question. Nothing says the course promises rewards, income, withdrawals, or unusual returns. The safety comments are consistent with responsible education and do not conceal a financial solicitation.

citations.quote: Users can access this course and more than 60 MasterClass courses by subscribing to the All-Access Pass for $180 per year.

opening.argument: The apparent educational interview also functions as promotion. The description presents a branded MasterClass, names where to find it, explains that access requires the All-Access Pass, and gives the annual price. That commercial call to action sits alongside the authority of a recognizable performer answering practical questions, so the educational framing can steer viewers toward purchase while appearing merely informative. At minimum, the content is promotional participation-oriented material rather than only neutral discussion.
